promptText: What does "concurrent" actually mean in React's rendering model, introduced in React 18 and unchanged in React 19?
options: Rendering became interruptible and priority-aware — React can pause, yield to the browser, and resume a render — while still running on a single thread
React began rendering multiple components in parallel across separate worker threads
Concurrent rendering means every state update is processed instantly with zero scheduling
It refers to Server Components running concurrently with Client Components on the same request
explanation: Concurrent does not mean multi-threaded or parallel; it means React's Fiber architecture makes rendering interruptible, so a render can be paused to let the browser handle higher-priority work, then resumed or discarded, all on a single thread.

promptText: Why does useOptimistic never require a manual rollback function in a catch block?
options: The optimistic value is derived fresh on every render from the current real state plus a pending guess, rather than being stored — so when the surrounding transition settles, the overlay simply stops being applied
React automatically retries the failed action up to three times before giving up
useOptimistic silently ignores any action that fails
The optimistic value is stored in a separate persistent cache that React clears on unmount
explanation: Because the optimistic state is computed as updateFn(realState, pendingGuess) on every render rather than stored separately, there's no 'previous value' to remember or explicitly revert — it disappears on its own once the transition finishes.

promptText: Why can the use() hook be called conditionally or after an early return, unlike useState or useEffect?
options: use() doesn't rely on call-order-based internal bookkeeping the way ordinary hooks do, so React doesn't need it invoked in the same order on every render
use() is not actually a React API — it's a plain JavaScript function with no special rules
Conditional hook calls have always been allowed for every hook since React 16
use() only works inside Server Components, where render order doesn't matter
explanation: use() is a deliberate, documented exception to the Rules of Hooks specifically because it doesn't depend on consistent call order the way useState's internal slot-based storage does, so each call is evaluated independently.

promptText: Before React 18, why would two setState calls inside a setTimeout callback trigger two separate re-renders instead of one?
options: Automatic batching only applied inside React's own event handlers; updates from a setTimeout, native listener, or promise callback each triggered an immediate render
setTimeout callbacks could not call setState at all prior to React 18
React always re-rendered once per setState call, even inside event handlers, before React 18
Batching required manually wrapping every setState call in an array
explanation: Prior to React 18, batching was scoped to React's own synthetic event handlers; updates triggered from a timeout, promise callback, or native listener each caused their own immediate render. React 18's createRoot made batching automatic everywhere.

promptText: Why does calling useFormStatus() inside the same component that renders the <form> element always return pending: false?
options: useFormStatus reads from the nearest ancestor form's context, and a component is not its own descendant — it's the ancestor providing that context, not a consumer of it
useFormStatus is deprecated and no longer functions in React 19
pending only becomes true after the form has been submitted at least twice
useFormStatus requires the form element to have a name attribute to report pending state
explanation: useFormStatus must be called from a genuine child of the form to read real pending/data/method/action values; calling it in the form's own component always returns the default, non-pending values because that component is the ancestor providing the context, not consuming it.

promptText: What is the key distinction between traditional SSR of a Client Component and a true Server Component?
options: SSR renders a Client Component's HTML on the server for a fast first paint but still ships its JS to hydrate afterward; a Server Component's code and dependencies never ship to the client at all, not even for the first paint
SSR and Server Components are two names for exactly the same mechanism introduced together in React 19
A Server Component is simply a Client Component that happens to render faster
SSR only works with Server Components, and Client Components cannot be server-rendered
explanation: SSR is about where the first HTML is generated; RSC is about whether a component's code ever reaches the client bundle at all. These are independent axes — a Client Component under SSR still ships its full JS bundle to hydrate, while a Server Component's code never runs in the browser under any circumstance.

promptText: Why must React's commit phase be synchronous and uninterruptible, while the render phase can be paused and resumed?
options: The commit phase applies changes directly to the real DOM and runs layout effects; a paused, half-applied DOM mutation would leave users seeing (and possibly interacting with) a structurally inconsistent tree, whereas an interrupted render phase has touched nothing observable yet
The commit phase is actually interruptible too, but React chooses not to interrupt it for historical reasons only
Synchronous commits are required only for backward compatibility with older browsers
The render phase is uninterruptible and the commit phase is the one that can be paused and resumed
explanation: Render-phase work is pure computation that produces nothing observable, so it's safe to pause, discard, or retry; commit is where DOM mutations and layout effects actually happen, and pausing mid-mutation would expose a visibly broken, inconsistent tree to the user.

promptText: A Client Component calls use(fetch('/api/items').then(r => r.json())) directly inside its render body. What bug does this introduce?
options: A brand-new promise is created on every render, so use() suspends on it, the component re-renders once it resolves, that re-render creates yet another new pending promise, and the cycle repeats indefinitely
fetch() cannot be called from inside a React component under any circumstances
The component will render exactly once and then permanently stop re-rendering
use() automatically caches the first promise's result by URL, so no bug actually occurs
explanation: The promise passed to use() needs a stable identity across renders. A bare fetch() call inline in render creates a fresh promise every time, so the component suspends, resolves, re-renders, creates a new promise, and suspends again forever — the fix is memoizing the promise or creating it once in a Server Component.

promptText: Why is a hand-rolled "subscribe in useEffect, mirror into useState" custom hook not fully safe under concurrent rendering, when reading from an external store?
options: The effect-based subscription only re-syncs after commit, leaving a window during an interrupted, resumed render where a component can read a stale snapshot inconsistent with a sibling reading the same store more recently — producing tearing
useEffect cannot read external variables at all under React 18 and later
useState updates triggered from inside useEffect are silently dropped under concurrent rendering
This pattern was safe under React 18 but was specifically broken by a change in React 19
explanation: Concurrent rendering can pause and resume a render, creating a window where an external (non-React-owned) store can change underneath it; an effect-based subscription only catches up after commit, so different components can render with inconsistent snapshots — exactly what useSyncExternalStore was built to prevent.

promptText: If a component violates the Rules of React (e.g. mutates a prop directly during render), what does the React Compiler do with that specific code?
options: It conservatively skips memoizing that specific piece of code, falling back to normal unmemoized behavior there, rather than guessing and risking a stale-value bug
It throws a hard build error that prevents the entire application from compiling
It silently rewrites the offending code to make it pure, without informing the developer
It disables all memoization across the entire application, not just the violating component
explanation: The compiler bails out conservatively per-value when it can't prove a piece of code is safe to memoize, rather than guessing — which is why a rule violation quietly loses an optimization rather than crashing the build, and why the companion lint plugin matters for catching it.

promptText: Why should an ErrorBoundary wrap a Suspense boundary (be its ancestor), rather than being nested inside it?
options: A rejected promise is an ordinary thrown error that propagates to the nearest ancestor error boundary, not something Suspense understands; if the error boundary were inside the Suspense boundary, a rejection occurring before it even mounts would have nothing local to catch it
React requires ErrorBoundary and Suspense to never appear in the same component tree at all
Suspense boundaries automatically convert all errors into pending states, so placement doesn't matter
Nesting order only affects which fallback UI displays visually first, not which one catches errors
explanation: Suspense only understands 'not ready yet' (a pending thrown promise); a rejected promise is an ordinary thrown error that must reach an ancestor error boundary. Placing the error boundary above the Suspense boundary ensures it's already mounted to catch a rejection, wherever in the pending-vs-failed outcome it lands.

promptText: A developer wraps both setQuery(value) (the input's own displayed value) and setFiltered(...) (an expensive list re-filter) inside the same startTransition call. What goes wrong?
options: The input's own value update inherits the transition's low priority along with the expensive computation, so typing itself can start to feel laggy — exactly the opposite of what transitions are meant to protect
startTransition throws a runtime error when more than one setState call appears inside it
Only the first setState call inside startTransition is applied; the second is silently ignored
React automatically detects which update is urgent and reorders them internally, so no problem actually occurs
explanation: Transitions only help when there's a genuine split between an urgent update and a non-urgent one; wrapping both in the same transition erases that split, so the urgent input update is now competing for the same low-priority scheduling slot as the expensive work, making the input itself feel laggy.

promptText: React represents update priority internally as a bitmask of named 'lanes' rather than a single numeric value. Concretely, what capability does this design choice provide that a single priority number would not?
options: A bitmask lets React efficiently represent and check combinations of pending work with fast bitwise operations (e.g. 'is there any sync work pending,' 'merge this into the same batch'), and lets multiple concurrent transitions occupy distinct lanes so they don't automatically block each other the way a single low-priority bucket would
Bitmasks are used purely for backward compatibility with React 17's numeric priority system and have no functional benefit in React 19
A bitmask allows React to run each lane's work on a genuinely separate CPU thread
Lanes exist only to label DevTools output and have no effect on actual scheduling behavior
explanation: Because a lane is a bit in a bitmask, React can cheaply combine and query sets of pending work rather than comparing single priority numbers one at a time, and multiple transitions can occupy separate transition lanes so unrelated low-priority updates don't necessarily block each other.

promptText: A Server Component calls getComments() without awaiting it and passes the raw promise down to a Client Component, which calls use(commentsPromise) inside its own Suspense boundary. What does this achieve that simply awaiting getComments() directly inside the Server Component would not?
options: It decouples where the fetch starts from where the loading state visually appears — the slow comments fetch runs in the background without blocking the Server Component's own output, letting the rest of the page render immediately while only the comments' own Suspense boundary waits
It causes the comments to load twice as fast because use() runs fetches on a separate thread from await
Awaiting directly inside a Server Component is not permitted by React at all, so this is the only valid way to fetch data
Passing an unawaited promise as a prop automatically converts the Client Component into a Server Component
explanation: An await in a Server Component blocks that component's own rendering; passing an unawaited promise down lets a Client Component descendant suspend its own, narrower boundary around the wait instead, which is exactly the mechanism behind independent per-section streaming.

promptText: What is the most defensible, interview-safe way to compare React's virtual-DOM diffing performance to a fine-grained reactivity framework like Solid or Svelte?
options: Fine-grained reactivity has genuinely lower constant-factor overhead for a single, isolated, already-known DOM update since it skips the re-render-and-diff discovery step entirely — but this narrow, true claim does not generalize to 'framework X is faster in real applications,' since real-world performance is dominated by architecture, bundle size, and whether React's concurrent features and Compiler are actually being used
React's virtual DOM is always faster than fine-grained reactivity because diffing is more CPU-efficient than dependency tracking
There is no meaningful performance difference between the two approaches under any circumstances, so the comparison isn't worth making
Fine-grained reactivity frameworks are strictly superior in every dimension, including ecosystem maturity and tooling
explanation: The precise, defensible claim separates a narrow true fact (lower constant-factor overhead for isolated, already-known updates in fine-grained frameworks) from an unsupported broad generalization (framework X is faster overall) — real application performance depends on far more than one micro-benchmark's update strategy.
